name: Enterprise asks
description: What enterprise customers ask startups for, what each takes to build or buy, and what to decide first.
note: Estimates are rough ranges written by hand, not measurements.

items.name: SSO
items.aka: Single sign-on with SAML and OIDC
items.what: Single sign-on lets a customer's employees log into your product with their company identity, from Okta, Microsoft Entra ID or Google Workspace, instead of a separate password. Two protocols matter. SAML 2.0 is what most enterprise IT teams still default to, and OIDC is newer and simpler. Either way, your product trusts the customer's identity provider to vouch for who someone is.
items.why_enterprises_ask: IT teams want one place to grant and revoke access. Without SSO, every employee who leaves keeps a working password to your product, and that is usually a hard blocker in security review.

cost_drivers.label: Customers set it up themselves, without your team
Existing password users need their accounts linked
SSO must be enforceable per org, with a break-glass login
Some customers need more than one identity provider

decide_first.question: Is SSO part of a paid tier, or a separate add-on?
decide_first.why: Decides whether this is revenue or a cost of doing business.

decide_first.question: When a customer turns SSO on, does password login switch off for their users?
decide_first.why: Enforcement is what security teams actually ask for, and it changes the migration.

decide_first.question: How do we match an SSO login to an existing account, and what happens when the emails don't match?
decide_first.why: Account linking is where most of the effort and most of the bugs live.

decide_first.question: Do we build it or buy it?
decide_first.why: The gap is roughly a month of engineering, plus ongoing maintenance per identity provider.

decide_first.question: What is the break-glass path if a customer's identity provider goes down?
decide_first.why: Someone has to be able to get in, and it can't be a backdoor.

decide_first.question: Which identity providers do the deals in our pipeline actually use?
decide_first.why: Tells you whether to start with SAML, OIDC or one specific provider.

decide_first.question: Who helps a customer's IT admin when setup fails?
decide_first.why: SSO setup is one of the most common first-week enterprise tickets.

items.name: SCIM
items.what: SCIM is a standard API that lets a customer's identity provider create, update and remove users in your product automatically. When IT adds someone to the right group in Okta or Entra ID, they appear in your app. When that person leaves the company, their access goes with them, and nobody has to file a ticket.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Removing access is a security control. Auditors check that departed employees lose access quickly, and doing it by hand doesn't pass.

cost_drivers.label: Directory groups need to map to roles in your product
It must be certified with Okta, Entra ID and Google
Removed users' data has retention or transfer rules
SSO isn't built yet, and usually comes first

decide_first.question: When someone is deprovisioned, do we suspend them or delete them?
decide_first.why: Suspending keeps their work and audit trail. Deleting can break things customers care about.

decide_first.question: Who owns content created by a user who has been removed?
decide_first.why: Customers will ask the day it first happens.

decide_first.question: How do directory groups map to roles in our product?
decide_first.why: Group mapping is what makes SCIM useful beyond creating accounts.

decide_first.question: What happens when a sync replays or arrives out of order?
decide_first.why: Identity providers retry, so sync has to be safe to run twice.

decide_first.question: How fast must access be removed after someone is offboarded?
decide_first.why: Minutes is the expectation, and auditors may test it.

decide_first.question: Is SCIM a hard requirement in current deals, or a nice-to-have?
decide_first.why: Decides whether this is this quarter's work.

items.name: RBAC
items.what: Role-based access control decides what each user is allowed to do. Instead of everyone being an admin or a member, users get roles, and each role carries specific permissions. Enterprise customers usually want to define their own roles, and to limit access to parts of the product, such as one region or one project.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Large companies run on least privilege and separation of duties. If your only options are admin and member, their security team will ask you to change that.

cost_drivers.label: Permission checks are scattered across the codebase today
Access must be scoped to resources, like projects or regions
Customers create their own roles in the UI
Every permission change must be audited

decide_first.question: Which roles do customers actually need on day one?
decide_first.why: Starting from real requests beats designing a perfect model nobody asked for.

decide_first.question: Can customers create custom roles, or only choose from ours?
decide_first.why: Custom roles roughly double the scope.

decide_first.question: Where do permission checks live today: backend, frontend, background jobs?
decide_first.why: If they're scattered, the inventory is the project.

decide_first.question: Do we need access scoped to specific resources, or only global roles?
decide_first.why: Scoping is the expensive half, and hard to retrofit.

decide_first.question: Who can grant admin, and is that change logged?
decide_first.why: Privilege escalation is the first thing a reviewer tests.

decide_first.question: What exact access request is blocking the current deal?
decide_first.why: One concrete request keeps the design honest.

items.name: Org hierarchy
items.what: Most products start with flat workspaces: one account, one set of users. A large company is a hierarchy instead, with a parent organisation, subsidiaries and business units that want their own data and admins under one contract. Supporting that means your data model can express parents, children and settings that pass down between them.
items.why_enterprises_ask: The biggest customers buy once and roll out many times. If each business unit needs its own separate account, you lose central admin and consolidated billing, and often the deal.

cost_drivers.label: Your data model assumes one flat workspace
Customers need to merge or split existing workspaces
Tenants need hard isolation, with separate databases or schemas

decide_first.question: Does a child org inherit settings from its parent, and can it override them?
decide_first.why: Inheritance rules decide almost every other design choice.

decide_first.question: Is billing consolidated at the parent, or per business unit?
decide_first.why: Billing and tenancy are easier to design together than to reconcile later.

decide_first.question: How many places in the code assume a user belongs to exactly one workspace?
decide_first.why: That assumption is the migration.

decide_first.question: What does tenant isolation mean for us: rows, schemas or databases?
decide_first.why: Each step up costs more and is harder to change later.

decide_first.question: Can a parent-org admin see data inside child orgs?
decide_first.why: Customers will ask, and the answer has legal consequences.

decide_first.question: Which prospect has the hierarchy, and what does it actually look like?
decide_first.why: Designing against a real org chart beats a hypothetical one.

items.name: SOC 2
items.what: SOC 2 is an audit report showing that your security controls exist and actually work. An independent CPA firm checks areas like access control, change management, monitoring and incident response against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. Type I looks at how the controls are designed at a single point in time. Type II checks that they operated over a period, usually three to twelve months, and Type II is the one enterprise buyers want.
items.why_enterprises_ask: It is the default proof of security when selling to US companies. Without it you'll answer long security questionnaires by hand, and some deals won't start.
items.calendar_note: Plan for six to nine months end to end. The Type II observation window is the long pole, not the engineering.

cost_drivers.label: No centralised logging or alerting today
Engineers have broad, standing access to production
No device management on company laptops
No written offboarding or access review process

decide_first.question: Which deals, by name, are waiting on SOC 2?
decide_first.why: Ties the work and its cost to revenue.

decide_first.question: Which systems are in scope, and which do we deliberately leave out?
decide_first.why: Tight scope is the biggest lever on effort.

decide_first.question: Who has production access today, and how is it granted?
decide_first.why: Access control is the most common audit finding.

decide_first.question: Who owns compliance day to day?
decide_first.why: If the answer is the CTO in their evenings, it slips.

decide_first.question: Type I first, or straight to Type II?
decide_first.why: Type I is faster to show buyers. Type II is what they actually want.

decide_first.question: Which audit firm, and when does the observation window start?
decide_first.why: The window sets the earliest date a report can exist.

items.name: ISO 27001
items.what: ISO 27001 is an international certification for how you manage information security. Instead of auditing individual controls the way SOC 2 does, it certifies a management system: how you assess risk, choose controls and keep improving them. An accredited certification body issues it on a three-year cycle, with a smaller surveillance audit each year.
items.why_enterprises_ask: It is the certification buyers in Europe and much of Asia expect. Many global enterprises accept either ISO 27001 or SOC 2, and some insist on ISO.
items.calendar_note: Typically four to nine months to certification, depending on how much already exists.

cost_drivers.label: You already hold SOC 2 (this reduces effort)
No documented risk assessment yet
The company operates in several countries

decide_first.question: Do our buyers require ISO specifically, or would SOC 2 do?
decide_first.why: Doing both before you need to is expensive.

decide_first.question: What is the scope: the product, or the whole company?
decide_first.why: Scope drives both effort and audit fees.

decide_first.question: Do we have a documented risk assessment and treatment plan?
decide_first.why: It's the core of ISO, and the part SOC 2 doesn't force.

decide_first.question: Who is the named owner of the management system?
decide_first.why: Certification bodies expect one accountable person.

decide_first.question: Can SOC 2 and ISO evidence run through one platform?
decide_first.why: Overlapping controls should only be collected once.

decide_first.question: Which accredited certification body will we use?
decide_first.why: Accreditation matters to buyers, and good bodies book up months ahead.

items.name: Audit logs
items.what: An audit log is a record of who did what, and when, inside your product: logins, permission changes, data exports, settings edits. Enterprise customers need to see it themselves, search it, export it and stream it into their own security tools, such as Splunk or Datadog. It has to be complete, hard to tamper with and kept for as long as their contract says.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Security teams investigate incidents with it, and auditors ask for it. Your internal application logs don't count, because customers can't see them and they aren't complete.

cost_drivers.label: Events must stream into the customer's SIEM
Events come from many different services
Retention must be configurable per contract

decide_first.question: Which actions must be logged on day one?
decide_first.why: Admin, login, permission and export events cover most requests.

decide_first.question: How many services would need to emit events?
decide_first.why: Coverage across services is the effort, not the storage.

decide_first.question: Do events have a stable, versioned schema?
decide_first.why: Customers build alerts on it, so changes break them.

decide_first.question: How long must logs be kept, and can anyone alter them?
decide_first.why: Retention and immutability are what auditors check.

decide_first.question: Do buyers want a UI, an export, or a SIEM stream?
decide_first.why: Those are three different amounts of work.

decide_first.question: Who explains a log entry when a customer asks?
decide_first.why: If events aren't self-explanatory, support pays for it.

items.name: Security questionnaire
items.what: A security questionnaire is the list of questions a buyer's security team sends before approving you as a vendor. Standard ones include SIG, CAIQ and HECVAT, and many companies send their own spreadsheet of a few hundred questions. They cover encryption, access control, incident response, subprocessors and more.
items.why_enterprises_ask: It sits between a verbal yes and a signed contract. Slow or inconsistent answers delay deals, and a wrong answer can end up written into the contract.

cost_drivers.label: More than one questionnaire arrives each month
Some answers depend on controls you haven't built yet
Public sector or regulated buyers with their own forms

decide_first.question: How many questionnaires arrived last quarter, and how long did each take?
decide_first.why: Volume decides whether this needs a tool or a spreadsheet.

decide_first.question: Who is allowed to answer, and who approves the answers?
decide_first.why: Wrong answers become contractual commitments.

decide_first.question: Which answers are currently 'no' or 'planned'?
decide_first.why: Those gaps are the real security roadmap.

decide_first.question: Can we publish a trust page with our policies and reports?
decide_first.why: A good trust page answers many questions before they're sent.

decide_first.question: What can we share under NDA, and what can be public?
decide_first.why: Pen test and SOC 2 reports usually need an NDA.

decide_first.question: Which questions keep coming back that a product change would answer?
decide_first.why: Repeated questions point at missing features.

items.name: Data residency
items.aka: GDPR, DPAs and keeping data in-region
items.what: Data residency means guaranteeing that a customer's data is stored and processed in a specific region, usually the EU. GDPR adds obligations on top: a data processing agreement, a published list of subprocessors, and handling requests to see or delete personal data. The hard part is that data rarely lives only in your main database. Logs, backups, analytics and support tools all hold copies.
items.why_enterprises_ask: European buyers often can't sign without a DPA, and some require EU hosting. A residency promise that turns out to be false is a breach of contract.

cost_drivers.label: You need a separate EU deployment of the product
Personal data sits in many third-party tools
Deletion must reach backups and analytics

decide_first.question: Do we offer a DPA today, and what does it already promise?
decide_first.why: It may commit you to things the system doesn't do yet.

decide_first.question: Where does customer data actually live, including logs, backups and analytics?
decide_first.why: The data map is the foundation for every residency claim.

decide_first.question: Does 'EU residency' mean the database, or everything?
decide_first.why: Buyers mean everything. Most systems only move the database.

decide_first.question: How do we handle a deletion request from start to finish?
decide_first.why: It has to reach every copy, within the legal deadline.

decide_first.question: Which subprocessors would we have to disclose?
decide_first.why: Adding one later means notifying customers.

decide_first.question: Which deals need EU hosting, and which only need a DPA?
decide_first.why: A DPA is paperwork. EU hosting is infrastructure.

items.name: HIPAA
items.what: HIPAA is the US law governing protected health information. If your product stores or processes health data for healthcare customers, you're a business associate: you sign a business associate agreement and meet the Security Rule's safeguards for access control, encryption, audit logging and breach notification. There is no official HIPAA certification. Buyers look at your controls, your BAA, and often a SOC 2 or HITRUST report.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Healthcare organisations legally can't share patient data with a vendor that won't sign a BAA.
items.calendar_note: Usually three to six months before you can sign a BAA with confidence.

cost_drivers.label: Health data flows into logs, analytics or support tools
Not all of your cloud services and vendors offer BAAs
Buyers also want HITRUST certification

decide_first.question: Will we sign BAAs, and on what terms?
decide_first.why: It is the legal gate for every healthcare deal.

decide_first.question: Which systems would touch protected health information?
decide_first.why: Keeping that footprint small is the cheapest control.

decide_first.question: Do all our vendors and cloud services sign BAAs with us?
decide_first.why: Any vendor that touches health data needs one.

decide_first.question: How would we detect and report a breach?
decide_first.why: Notification has legal deadlines.

decide_first.question: Do we actually need health data, or can the product work without it?
decide_first.why: Not storing it is the best compliance strategy there is.

decide_first.question: Are buyers asking for HITRUST, or is a BAA plus SOC 2 enough?
decide_first.why: HITRUST is a much bigger program.

items.name: BYOK
items.aka: Bring your own key, or customer-managed encryption keys
items.what: BYOK lets a customer control the key that encrypts their data inside your product, usually held in their own AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS or Azure Key Vault. Your system uses their key to encrypt and decrypt, and if they revoke it, their data becomes unreadable, including to you. It is typically built with envelope encryption: per-tenant data keys, wrapped by the customer's master key.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Banks, healthcare companies and large enterprises want the ability to cut off access to their data, including from their vendors.

cost_drivers.label: Support for more than one cloud KMS
Search or analytics must still work over encrypted data
Existing data must be re-encrypted

decide_first.question: What happens to the product when a customer revokes their key?
decide_first.why: Revocation has to fail safely, without corrupting data.

decide_first.question: Which data is encrypted with the customer's key: everything, or specific fields?
decide_first.why: Scope decides both effort and performance cost.

decide_first.question: Which key management services do our buyers use?
decide_first.why: Each one is its own integration.

decide_first.question: How are keys rotated, and who can trigger it?
decide_first.why: Rotation is where designs quietly break.

decide_first.question: Has BYOK already been promised in a contract?
decide_first.why: Promised before it was scoped is a common trap.

decide_first.question: Is BYOK an enterprise add-on?
decide_first.why: It has real ongoing cost, and is usually priced.

items.name: Penetration test
items.what: A penetration test is an authorised attack on your product by an outside security firm, looking for weaknesses before someone else finds them. The firm tests your application, APIs and infrastructure, then delivers a report of findings ranked by severity. Enterprise buyers usually ask for a summary letter or report from a test in the last twelve months.
items.why_enterprises_ask: It is independent evidence that your security holds up, and a standard item in both security questionnaires and SOC 2 audits.
items.calendar_note: Book two to six weeks ahead. The test itself takes one to three weeks, and fixing findings takes as long as it takes.

cost_drivers.label: Findings include high or critical issues to fix
Scope includes mobile apps or infrastructure
Buyers want a retest letter showing fixes

decide_first.question: What's in scope: web app, APIs, infrastructure, mobile?
decide_first.why: Scope drives both price and usefulness.

decide_first.question: Who is free to fix findings in the weeks afterwards?
decide_first.why: An unfixed critical finding is worse than no report.

decide_first.question: Do we test production, or a staging copy?
decide_first.why: Staging is safer and production is more honest. Decide on purpose.

decide_first.question: What do we share with customers: the full report, a summary or a letter?
decide_first.why: Most companies share a summary under NDA.

decide_first.question: Which deals need the report, and by when?
decide_first.why: Firms book up, so the deadline sets the timeline.

decide_first.question: Once a year, or continuous testing and a bug bounty?
decide_first.why: Different costs, and a different signal to buyers.

items.name: Usage-based billing
items.what: Usage-based billing charges customers for what they use: API calls, active seats, compute, messages. It needs a metering pipeline that records usage accurately, rates it against each customer's contract, and turns it into invoices. Enterprise contracts often combine usage with a committed minimum, prepaid credits and overage rates.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Buyers want to pay in line with value, and their finance teams want to forecast. Both depend on meters you can trust and invoices you can explain.

cost_drivers.label: Contracts mix commits, credits and overage
Customers see their usage in near real time
Existing customers are migrating off seat-based pricing

decide_first.question: What is the one value metric we charge on?
decide_first.why: Every other design choice follows from it.

decide_first.question: Can we rebuild any invoice line from raw usage events?
decide_first.why: Disputes and audits both require it.

decide_first.question: What happens if usage events are late, duplicated or lost?
decide_first.why: Meters need replay and deduplication to be trusted.

decide_first.question: How do commits, credits and overages show up on invoices and in revenue?
decide_first.why: Finance has to recognise the revenue correctly.

decide_first.question: What will we let sales discount or customise?
decide_first.why: Bespoke deal structures break billing systems.

decide_first.question: How does a customer see their current usage?
decide_first.why: Surprise bills cause churn.

items.name: Enterprise invoicing
items.aka: Contracts, purchase orders and net terms
items.what: Self-serve products charge a card on a subscription. Enterprise customers pay invoices instead: annual or multi-year contracts, purchase order numbers, net 30 or net 60 terms, payment by bank transfer, and pricing that changes over time with ramps and true-ups. Billing has to model the contract, not just the plan.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprise procurement often can't pay by card at all. And contracts your billing can't represent end up managed in spreadsheets, which is where invoices go wrong.

cost_drivers.label: Multi-year deals with ramps or quarterly true-ups
Invoices must sync to your accounting system
Mid-term upgrades need proration

decide_first.question: Which contract terms do we actually sell today?
decide_first.why: Model the real ones first, not every possible one.

decide_first.question: Who edits invoices by hand, and how often?
decide_first.why: Manual edits show exactly where the model is missing something.

decide_first.question: What can sales change in an order form without approval?
decide_first.why: Every exception becomes a billing edge case.

decide_first.question: How does a signed contract switch on features in the product?
decide_first.why: Billing and entitlements drift apart without a link.

decide_first.question: Do our terms support purchase orders, net terms and auto-renewal?
decide_first.why: Procurement will redline them otherwise.

decide_first.question: Who answers when a customer disputes a line on an invoice?
decide_first.why: Explaining an invoice needs data behind every line.

items.name: Entitlements
items.what: Entitlements decide which features and limits each customer has, based on what they bought. A good entitlement system is one source of truth that the product checks, instead of plan names hardcoded throughout the code. It lets you create an enterprise tier, sell add-ons and give one customer a custom limit without a code deploy.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprise deals come with custom packaging. Without entitlements, every deal turns into an engineering ticket.

cost_drivers.label: Plan checks are hardcoded across the codebase
Contracts grant custom limits or features per customer
Entitlements must stay in sync with billing

decide_first.question: What's in each tier, and what's an add-on?
decide_first.why: Write the packaging down before building the thing that enforces it.

decide_first.question: How do we move a feature from one tier to another?
decide_first.why: It will happen, and it shouldn't need a migration.

decide_first.question: Where does the product check plans today?
decide_first.why: Scattered checks are the migration.

decide_first.question: How often do deals include custom limits?
decide_first.why: Frequent exceptions justify self-serve overrides.

decide_first.question: Is billing or the entitlement system the source of truth?
decide_first.why: Two sources of truth eventually disagree.

decide_first.question: Can support see what a customer is entitled to?
decide_first.why: Otherwise every access question needs an engineer.

items.name: Single-tenant deployment
items.what: Some customers won't use a shared, multi-tenant service. Single-tenant options range from a dedicated instance you run for one customer, to deploying into the customer's own cloud account, to on-premises or fully air-gapped installs you never see. Each step moves more operational work into environments you don't control.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Regulated industries, governments and large enterprises often require data to stay inside their environment. For them, shared SaaS is a non-starter.

cost_drivers.label: The customer runs it, not you
Fully air-gapped, with offline installs and licensing
Several targets: AWS, GCP, Azure or bare metal

decide_first.question: Is this one deal, or a product line we'll sell again?
decide_first.why: One-offs rarely pay for their ongoing cost.

decide_first.question: What do we charge for it?
decide_first.why: Dedicated deployments usually price at a multiple of list, and need to.

decide_first.question: Can every deployment ship from one artifact and one release train?
decide_first.why: Forked versions are the long-term cost.

decide_first.question: How do upgrades happen without one of our engineers on a call?
decide_first.why: Customer-run environments drift behind otherwise.

decide_first.question: How do we debug an environment we can't access?
decide_first.why: Support needs logs and diagnostics built in from the start.

decide_first.question: What does the customer's security team require of the install?
decide_first.why: Their requirements set the architecture.

items.name: Admin console
items.what: An admin console is where a customer's administrators run your product for their company without contacting you: managing users and roles, configuring SSO, setting security policies and viewing usage and billing. Enterprise admins also expect some control over change, such as advance notice of updates and the ability to delay a rollout to their users.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Large customers can't file a support ticket for every admin task. Self-service administration is what makes the product manageable at their size.

cost_drivers.label: Admin tasks run through internal tools or support tickets today
Customers need per-org control over feature rollouts
Every admin action must also be available through the API

decide_first.question: Which admin tasks create the most support tickets?
decide_first.why: That's your priority order.

decide_first.question: Do customers need to delay or schedule product changes?
decide_first.why: Change control is a common enterprise request that's easy to miss.

decide_first.question: Can we build the console on the same API customers would use?
decide_first.why: It gets you API parity for free.

decide_first.question: Which admin actions need extra confirmation or logging?
decide_first.why: Admin consoles are a high-value target.

decide_first.question: What can support do on a customer's behalf, and is it logged?
decide_first.why: Acting as a customer needs clear limits.

decide_first.question: What does the buyer's IT team expect to manage themselves?
decide_first.why: Their checklist is usually specific.

items.name: Public API
items.what: A public API lets customers automate your product and connect it to their other systems. For enterprise use that means stable, versioned endpoints, authentication with scoped tokens, documented rate limits, and webhooks that tell their systems when something changes. Once customers build on it, changing it breaks them, so the API becomes a long-term commitment.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprises run dozens of tools and expect them to connect. Integrations and automation are often part of the evaluation, not an afterthought.

cost_drivers.label: Your app's internal endpoints would need redesigning first
Webhooks need retries, signing and replay
Customers need OAuth apps, not just API keys

decide_first.question: Which five workflows do customers most want to automate?
decide_first.why: Start with those, not with everything.

decide_first.question: What's our deprecation policy?
decide_first.why: Enterprise customers expect around twelve months' notice.

decide_first.question: Are we exposing internal endpoints, or designing a separate surface?
decide_first.why: Internal endpoints change with your UI, and break customers when they do.

decide_first.question: What rate limits reflect our real capacity?
decide_first.why: Limits should protect you without surprising customers.

decide_first.question: How are tokens scoped, rotated and revoked?
decide_first.why: API tokens are credentials with broad reach.

decide_first.question: Which integrations come up in deals most often?
decide_first.why: Tells you what to build yourselves.

items.name: Data export
items.what: Enterprise customers want two things from their data in your product: reports that show the value they're getting, and a way to get raw data into their own warehouse. The first means dashboards for admins and executives. The second means scheduled exports or direct syncs into Snowflake, BigQuery or S3 that their analysts can build on.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Renewals are argued with data. The executive who signs off on the renewal rarely logs in, so the reporting has to reach them.

cost_drivers.label: Customers want direct warehouse syncs, not CSV files
Reports need custom metrics per customer
Data volumes are large, or needed in near real time

decide_first.question: What outcome did the customer buy, and how do we measure it?
decide_first.why: Reports should prove the value that was sold.

decide_first.question: Who reads the reports: admins, analysts or executives?
decide_first.why: Each needs a different format.

decide_first.question: Which warehouses do our customers use?
decide_first.why: Snowflake and BigQuery cover most, but check.

decide_first.question: Are our metric definitions written down and stable?
decide_first.why: Two dashboards that disagree destroy trust.

decide_first.question: What data is allowed to leave our systems in an export?
decide_first.why: Exports are a data-loss path, and customers ask about it.

decide_first.question: What data do customers ask for in business reviews today?
decide_first.why: It's a ready-made spec.

items.name: SLA
items.aka: Service level agreement: uptime and support commitments
items.what: An SLA is a contractual promise about your service: usually an uptime percentage, support response times by severity, and credits if you miss them. 99.9% uptime allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, and 99.99% allows about four. Behind the number you need monitoring that measures uptime the way customers experience it, and a support team staffed to meet the response times.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprises depend on your product for their own work. An SLA shows you'll stand behind it, and procurement often won't sign without one.

cost_drivers.label: Promising 99.99% or higher, which means multi-region failover
24/7 response for top-severity issues
Service credits calculated and applied automatically

decide_first.question: What has our availability actually been, measured from the customer's side?
decide_first.why: Never sign a number you haven't measured.

decide_first.question: What would the proposed credits have cost us over the last year?
decide_first.why: Replaying real history shows the true exposure.

decide_first.question: Who responds to a severity-one issue at 3am?
decide_first.why: Response times need a staffed rota, not a promise.

decide_first.question: What counts as downtime: a full outage, degraded service, or one feature failing?
decide_first.why: Definitions decide whether you owe credits.

decide_first.question: Are credits the only remedy, and are they capped?
decide_first.why: Uncapped liability is a common redline.

decide_first.question: What number are buyers asking for, and would 99.9% do?
decide_first.why: Buyers accept 99.9% more often than teams expect.

items.name: Enterprise onboarding
items.what: Enterprise onboarding is everything between a signed contract and thousands of people actually using the product: migrating data from the tool you're replacing, importing users in bulk, configuring SSO and roles, training admins and rolling out in phases. It usually runs as a project with milestones on both sides, and is sometimes sold as professional services.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Large accounts that stall after signing don't renew. Whether a customer sees value is decided in roughly the first sixty days.

cost_drivers.label: Data must be migrated from a competitor's product
Rollout covers thousands of users across business units
You plan to sell implementation as paid services

decide_first.question: What does a successful first sixty days look like, in numbers?
decide_first.why: Without a target, onboarding never finishes.

decide_first.question: What do the customer's admins need to be trained on?
decide_first.why: Admins who don't understand the product can't roll it out.

decide_first.question: Can customers import and check their own data?
decide_first.why: Self-service tooling keeps engineers out of every rollout.

decide_first.question: Who owns the implementation plan on our side?
decide_first.why: Enterprise rollouts need a named owner.

decide_first.question: What did we promise about timelines and support during the sale?
decide_first.why: Implementation inherits every promise.

decide_first.question: Is implementation included, or sold as services?
decide_first.why: Unpriced services quietly eat margin.

items.name: RAG
items.what: Retrieval-augmented generation answers a question by first finding the relevant passages in a customer's own content, then giving only those passages to a language model to write the answer. Content is split into chunks, turned into embeddings and stored in a vector index. Done well, answers cite their sources and stay inside what the customer's documents actually say.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprise buyers want answers grounded in their data, not the model's general knowledge. They also need to know one customer's documents can never surface in another customer's answers.

cost_drivers.label: Documents carry permissions that answers must respect
Content lives in many sources, like Drive, Confluence and Slack
Answers must cite sources a user can check
Data must stay in one region or in the customer's cloud

decide_first.question: What questions should it answer well, and which should it refuse?
decide_first.why: A written scope is the only way to judge whether it works.

decide_first.question: How does retrieval respect each user's permissions on the source documents?
decide_first.why: An answer built from a document someone can't open is a data leak.

decide_first.question: How will we know when a change to chunking or embeddings made answers worse?
decide_first.why: Without an evaluation set, every tweak is a guess.

decide_first.question: How are each tenant's indexes kept apart?
decide_first.why: Cross-tenant retrieval is the first thing a reviewer will probe.

decide_first.question: Which model providers see customer content, and do they retain it?
decide_first.why: They go on your subprocessor list and into the DPA.

decide_first.question: Do buyers need citations before they'll trust the answers?
decide_first.why: Citations change the design, and they're hard to add later.

items.name: Evals
items.what: Evals are tests for AI features. You collect realistic inputs with known good outcomes, run the feature against them, and score the results automatically: with code, with another model acting as a judge, or with human review. They tell you whether a prompt change, a new model or a retrieval tweak made things better or worse before customers find out.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprise buyers ask how you know the AI is accurate and how you catch regressions. A pass rate on a real set of tasks is a far better answer than a demo.

cost_drivers.label: No labelled examples of good answers exist yet
Quality needs expert human review, not just automated scoring
Evals must run on every deploy and block bad releases

decide_first.question: What does a good answer look like, written down precisely enough to score?
decide_first.why: If you can't define it, you can't measure it.

decide_first.question: Which failures are unacceptable, and which are merely annoying?
decide_first.why: Scoring should weight the failures customers actually care about.

decide_first.question: Where do eval cases come from, and how do real production failures get added?
decide_first.why: An eval set that never grows stops reflecting reality.

decide_first.question: If a model grades the answers, how did we check the grader?
decide_first.why: An unchecked judge can hide the very problems it's meant to catch.

decide_first.question: Would we share eval results with buyers?
decide_first.why: Published numbers build trust, and commit you to maintaining them.

decide_first.question: How do bad answers reported by customers end up in the eval set?
decide_first.why: Every complaint should become a test.

items.name: AI guardrails
items.aka: Prompt injection defences and output controls
items.what: Guardrails are the checks around an AI feature that stop it being misused or saying something it shouldn't. They screen inputs for prompt injection, where hidden instructions in a document or message try to take over the model, redact sensitive data, and check outputs before they reach a user or trigger an action. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications is where most security teams start.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Security reviewers now ask specifically about prompt injection and data leaking through AI features. Without a good answer, the AI feature can block the whole deal.

cost_drivers.label: The AI reads untrusted content, like emails, web pages or uploads
The AI can take actions, not just answer
Regulated data must be redacted before it reaches a model

decide_first.question: What is the worst thing the AI could be tricked into doing?
decide_first.why: Guardrails should be sized to the real blast radius.

decide_first.question: Has anyone tried to break it on purpose?
decide_first.why: Red teaming finds what checklists miss.

decide_first.question: Which content reaching the model could contain instructions written by outsiders?
decide_first.why: That's where prompt injection comes from.

decide_first.question: What can the model access or change, and is that the minimum it needs?
decide_first.why: Least privilege limits the damage when a guardrail fails.

decide_first.question: Who is accountable when a filtered answer is still wrong or harmful?
decide_first.why: Decide it before it happens.

decide_first.question: Do users see why something was blocked?
decide_first.why: Silent blocking looks like a bug.

items.name: LLM observability
items.aka: Tracing, cost and quality monitoring for AI features
items.what: LLM observability records what an AI feature actually did in production: the prompt, the retrieved context, the model's response, any tool calls, latency, token cost and user feedback, all linked together as one trace. It's how teams debug a bad answer, notice quality drifting and explain a surprising bill.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Enterprise customers expect a bad AI answer to be investigated like any other incident. They also ask what gets logged, because prompts usually contain their data.

cost_drivers.label: Prompts contain customer data needing redaction or short retention
Customers need traces for their own audits
Several models and providers are in use

decide_first.question: Can we reconstruct exactly what happened for any single answer?
decide_first.why: It's the first thing you need when a customer escalates.

decide_first.question: What does each AI feature cost per customer, per month?
decide_first.why: AI costs grow with usage and can quietly erase margin.

decide_first.question: What do traces store, for how long, and who can see them?
decide_first.why: Prompt logs are customer data.

decide_first.question: How do users tell us an answer was wrong?
decide_first.why: Feedback is the cheapest quality signal you'll get.

decide_first.question: Do we pass AI costs on, cap them, or absorb them?
decide_first.why: Pricing needs to know before usage takes off.

decide_first.question: Can support look up a customer's AI interaction without an engineer?
decide_first.why: Otherwise every AI ticket escalates.

items.name: AI data controls
items.aka: What the model sees, keeps and learns from
items.what: AI data controls answer the questions every enterprise legal team now asks. Is our data used to train models? Which model providers see it, and do they keep it? Can we switch AI features off, or keep processing in our region? The answers live partly in contracts with model providers, partly in settings customers control, and partly in how the system is built.
items.why_enterprises_ask: It's often the first AI question in procurement, and a vague answer stalls the deal. Some companies block AI features entirely until these controls exist.

cost_drivers.label: Admins must be able to switch AI features off per workspace
AI processing must stay in the customer's region
Some customers want to bring their own model or API key

decide_first.question: Is customer data ever used to train or improve models, ours or a provider's?
decide_first.why: Buyers will want the answer in writing.

decide_first.question: Which AI providers are subprocessors, and what do they retain?
decide_first.why: They belong on the subprocessor list and in the DPA.

decide_first.question: When an admin turns AI off, does all data stop flowing to models?
decide_first.why: An off switch that doesn't stop the data isn't one.

decide_first.question: Where are prompts, context and outputs stored, and for how long?
decide_first.why: Retention promises have to match the system.

decide_first.question: Could one customer's data influence another customer's answers?
decide_first.why: Shared caches, fine-tunes and indexes are common leak paths.

decide_first.question: How many deals now include AI restrictions in the contract?
decide_first.why: Tells you whether these controls are table stakes yet.

items.name: AI governance
items.aka: ISO 42001, the EU AI Act and responsible AI reviews
items.what: AI governance is how you show AI features are built and run responsibly: an AI policy, a risk assessment for each feature, a record of which models are used and how, human oversight where it matters, and a process for incidents. ISO/IEC 42001 certifies an AI management system, the EU AI Act places obligations on certain uses, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a common reference in the US.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Large buyers now run AI-specific vendor reviews alongside security reviews. Regulated customers especially need evidence they can show their own auditors.
items.calendar_note: Plan for four to nine months to ISO 42001 certification if you already run a security programme.

cost_drivers.label: You already hold ISO 27001 (this reduces effort)
An AI feature could fall into a regulated or high-risk use
Buyers want an AI-specific questionnaire answered

decide_first.question: Could any of our AI features count as high-risk under the EU AI Act?
decide_first.why: It decides how much of the Act applies.

decide_first.question: Where does a person review or approve what the AI does?
decide_first.why: Human oversight is central to every framework.

decide_first.question: Do we keep a record of which models and versions each feature uses?
decide_first.why: It's the first thing an assessor asks for.

decide_first.question: How would we detect and respond to an AI incident?
decide_first.why: Frameworks expect a process, not an apology.

decide_first.question: Are buyers asking for ISO 42001, or only for answers to AI questions?
decide_first.why: Certification is a much bigger commitment than a questionnaire.

decide_first.question: Who owns AI governance, and can it sit inside existing compliance work?
decide_first.why: Running it separately doubles the effort.

items.name: Agent permissions
items.aka: Letting AI agents act safely on a user's behalf
items.what: Agent permissions control what an AI agent can do when it acts for someone: which tools and APIs it can call, whose data it can touch, and which actions need a person to approve first. The safe pattern is to give the agent the acting user's permissions and no more, keep credentials out of the model's reach, log every action, and require approval before anything destructive or irreversible.
items.why_enterprises_ask: Buyers are comfortable with AI that drafts and suggests. They get nervous when it can send, delete or pay, and they'll ask exactly how that's contained.

cost_drivers.label: Agents act in third-party tools like email, CRM or payments
Some actions need a person to approve before they run
Customers must be able to see and undo what an agent did

decide_first.question: Which actions can an agent take on its own, and which need a person to approve?
decide_first.why: That line is the heart of the design.

decide_first.question: Does the agent act with the user's permissions, or broader ones of its own?
decide_first.why: Broad service credentials turn one mistake into a breach.

decide_first.question: Where are credentials for connected tools stored, and can the model ever see them?
decide_first.why: Secrets that reach the prompt can leak through the output.

decide_first.question: How would we stop an agent that's been manipulated by prompt injection?
decide_first.why: An agent that can act is the highest-stakes injection target.

decide_first.question: Can a customer see a log of every action an agent took?
decide_first.why: Trust depends on being able to check.

decide_first.question: Who is responsible when an agent takes the wrong action?
decide_first.why: Decide it before a customer asks.
